access.accountWall: The real consultation was never reached (security checkpoint before the first question), so the exact place of the sign-in step is not seen. Older app code puts it after the anonymous quiz, the recommendation, the format and plan-length choice and the add-ons, at /checkout/email ('Create an account': first name, last name, email, phone number, date of birth, password), followed by a medical-history questionnaire, hair photos and the order review. On both landing-page pop-ups (men and women) the wall is an email box straight after one picture question: the 'eligible / not eligible' verdict is only shown after an email is given. Voy's help-centre articles also need sign-in.
blockers: www.joinvoy.com and manual.co: Vercel security checkpoint, HTTP 429 'Failed to verify your browser, Code 21'. Re-tested once in stage 2 on /n/hair-loss/quiz, /n/hair-loss/quiz/gateway and /n/female-hair-loss/quiz (runs/s2-retest-men, runs/s2-retest-gateway, runs/s2-probe-female-quiz) and through the web-fetch tool (HTTP 429). Not worked around. Stage 3 re-tested once more: /n/hair-loss/quiz and /n/female-hair-loss/quiz gave the same checkpoint in the browser (runs/verify-base-men, runs/verify-base-women), and web fetch got HTTP 429 on the quiz and on a product page.

Voy help centre (joinvoy.zendesk.com) and old Manual help centre: hair-loss articles redirect to a sign-in page; web fetch gets HTTP 403. Not signed in. Stage 3: two help-centre articles again answered HTTP 403 to web fetch.

Wayback Machine: a copy of /n/hair-loss/quiz from 17 Aug 2026 exists, but web.archive.org cannot be reached from this machine (the outbound connection is closed) and the web-fetch tool refuses that site. archive.ph: same. Common Crawl index: time-outs (HTTP 504) and closed connections on every query.

The quiz questions are not in any file that could be read: older app code shows they are downloaded at run time from an address under /shop-api/ on the blocked host. That address was not called (only addresses an anonymous page called by itself are allowed).
access.coverageNote: No real quiz screen was seen, in stage 1 or stage 2. Live replays (20 in stage 2, 3 of them blocked access checks) cover only what Voy serves without the checkpoint: the men's landing-page pop-up (6 options), the women's landing-page pop-up (4 options and Skip) and the men's pattern picker (6 options), each option on its own. Site code covers (a) the scripts of those landing pages, which hold the pop-ups' eligibility rule, and (b) a copy of the older Manual web app's shared script (29 Dec 2025, from a public web archive), which holds the quiz ENGINE (how answers remove products or reject the patient, how follow-up questions are shown, the order of the funnel pages) but not the questions. Public documents cover Voy's own landing pages for men and women (read live on Voy's public hosts hairloss1.joinvoy.com and femalehairloss1.joinvoy.com), older Manual treatment-plan pages with full 'who should not take it' lists (archive copies), terms of sale, GPhC reports and Manual's published service evaluation. Help-centre and www.joinvoy.com product pages were read only through search-engine summaries. Every quiz-related entry says which of these it rests on. Stage 3 (verification) replayed every baseline and six stage 2 experiments again with the same results, re-read the page scripts and the archived app code, and added 13 gap replays: the older Manual plan picker that is still online (format and plan length, the only product chooser that works without the blocked app), the page aimed at both sexes, the women's /meta pop-up, the product-first landing page and the coupon hand-over. None of these is the consultation itself.

engineSummary: Voy's real quiz could not be opened in any of the three stages, so this is the engine only as far as public evidence shows it. What was seen: (1) A pattern gate before the quiz. The men's and women's landing pages open a one-question pop-up. Its own script refuses 'Patchy' and 'Complete' (men) and 'Patchy hair loss' (women) with 'You aren't eligible', and sends everyone else to the quiz with a discount code attached. The verdict only appears after an email is given; ticking a refused option looks exactly like ticking an accepted one. The page aimed at both sexes shows the men's picture question to everyone. A separate pattern picker is pure marketing: every pattern leads to the same quiz link. (2) On an older Manual page that is still online, choosing 'Spray' instead of 'Tablets' switches the product (minoxidil capsules to 10% spray) at the same price, and choosing 3 months instead of 6 changes only the price and pack size. What was read in code, not seen running: an 11-month-old copy of the same web app (Manual, December 2025). There the quiz starts with a list of products, and each question can carry a reject list (one matching answer leaves no product and shows 'You aren't eligible', with a 'Review your answers' button), an exclude list (the answer removes named products and the quiz carries on) and parent or JSON Logic conditions (the answer opens, hides or rewords later questions). In that function an answer can only remove products, never add one. Which answers sit on which list is in a definition the app downloads at run time; it could not be read, and that code has no women's hair flow in it. What Voy publishes: lists of who should not have which medicine. DHT blockers (finasteride, dutasteride) are 'not suitable' for men trying for a baby or with a pregnant partner, men treated for an enlarged prostate, men who have had breast or prostate cancer, and men with severe depression; minoxidil 'should not be used' with low or uncontrolled blood pressure or a sore scalp, or over 65; under-18s, women (in the men's service) and men who are completely bald or do not have pattern hair loss are not treated. Whether the quiz applies each of these by removing a product, by warning, or by leaving it to the clinician was not seen. After the quiz, older code and Voy's pages point to: a recommendation (Voy leads with finasteride plus minoxidil together for men; women are offered minoxidil only, as serum or tablets, at a strength the clinician sets), a format and plan-length choice, add-ons (shampoo, vitamins), then the account, a medical-history questionnaire, photos and payment details, and a prescriber's review that sees flagged and changed answers. Older terms say payment is taken only on approval.
strengths: A wide men's range: licensed finasteride, 10% (and probably 5%) minoxidil spray, 2.5 mg oral minoxidil, one-a-day combined capsules (finasteride with minoxidil; a dutasteride version is described in the help centre) and, on older pages, a topical finasteride + minoxidil spray. Voy advertises '30+ treatment combinations'. No comparison with other companies was made in this file.

An engine that can keep the customer: in the older code an answer can remove one medicine and leave the rest on offer, and a swap flag exists on the product-first route (what it does is inferred). How often Voy uses removal rather than refusal is not known; the only refusals seen are the pattern gate in the pop-ups.

Low entry prices in adverts (from £13 to £19 a month for men, £14.99 to £15 for women on first order), payment only after clinician approval (older terms of sale), a 180-day Money Back Promise, 'unlimited clinician support' and a photo progress tracker.

One-pill-a-day and once-a-day-spray formats that are easy to stick to; its own published 502-patient evaluation of the combined capsule; full written treatment plans with clear 'who should not take it' and fertility sections.
A women's service under the same roof with its own dermatologist lead, a strength set per patient and an offer to remove an active a woman is allergic to.

Own pharmacy and in-house prescribers, delivery advertised in under 48 hours, pause / switch / cancel in the account, and heavy conversion testing (70 experiment and feature flags downloaded by the landing page on the day).
weaknesses: The eligibility pop-up takes the email first and gives the verdict second: someone with patchy or complete loss hands over contact details only to be told 'You aren't eligible', with no explanation, advice or referral.
Marketing contradicts the gate: the pattern picker promises results for the most advanced stage (50% to 63% 'saw regrowth') while the pop-up refuses complete loss.

Diagnosis looks thin, as far as public material shows (the quiz itself was not seen): a picture choice and a medical history taking 'under 2 minutes'. Nothing public mentions questions on shedding speed, diet, iron, thyroid, hormones or medicines that cause hair loss; photos are described as for tracking, not for diagnosis before the first prescription.

Thin women's range: minoxidil only (serum or tablets) plus vitamins, for every cause Voy itself lists (hormonal, menopause, postpartum, stress). No blood test is mentioned on the hair-loss pages, although the company sells them for other services. The page aimed at both sexes shows women the men's picture question.

Regulatory record of the pharmacy: GPhC found standards not all met in March and August 2026 (answers not independently verified; clinical checks on only a sample; unlawful advertising of prescription-only medicines), with enforcement, before a clean re-inspection in October 2026. The 'review your answers' button on the refusal screen is the kind of answer-changing the regulator worries about, even though changes are logged.

Opaque: medicine names are hidden on ad pages ('Hair Oral Treatment', 'DHT blockers'), several products are unlicensed specials without that being said up front, strengths for women are not published, and the help centre is locked behind sign-in.

Headline prices are first-order promotions on a 6-month plan: the complete plan is advertised 'from £19' but bills at £33.17 a month on 6-month billing and £44 on monthly billing (search summary of the plan page). Pages contradict each other (women's serum: £14.99, £24 and £39; spray 'once a day' on one page and 'twice daily' on another), and the page code holds a hidden test that would show '£33' struck through beside every men's price.
opportunities: Give the verdict before asking for contact details, and never dead-end: for patchy, sudden or complete loss explain the likely causes and route to a clinician review, a GP letter or a dermatology referral.

Diagnose properly where Voy appears only to screen (its quiz could not be seen): ask about speed of loss, shedding, scalp symptoms, periods and menopause, recent illness, diet and medicines; use baseline photos reviewed by a clinician before the first prescription; offer ferritin, thyroid and hormone tests when the answers point that way.

Build a real women's pathway (cause work-up, topical and oral minoxidil at stated strengths, spironolactone and other anti-androgens where appropriate, menopause link, postpartum advice) instead of one medicine for every cause.

Be transparent where Voy is not: every active and strength, licensed or unlicensed status, the standing price for each plan length and the full eligibility rules, all visible before any email is asked for.

Make safety a feature: verify key answers (GP summary or NHS App record, blood-pressure reading before oral minoxidil), run structured mood and sexual side-effect check-ins on DHT blockers (Voy's own study admits it had none), and explain refusals instead of offering a 'review your answers' button.

Offer what Voy does not: lower-dose and stepwise oral minoxidil, topical-only DHT-blocker routes with clear strengths for men who fear tablets, options for men trying to conceive, and care for over-65s rather than a blanket exclusion.

verification.verdict: Trust this report for three things: (1) what Voy shows in public before the quiz (the pop-up gates and their rules, the pattern picker, landing prices and product names, the women's offer), which was replayed again in stage 3 with the same results; (2) how the older Manual app's engine worked in December 2025, which was read in the code twice; and (3) which exclusions Voy publishes. Do not read it as a map of Voy's consultation. No quiz screen was reached in any stage because of a security checkpoint that was deliberately not worked around, so there is no question list, no option-by-option rule and no observed recommendation for the real quiz. The rules that tie a medical answer to a product are published cautions or reasoning from them, now labelled as such, and several strengths and prices rest on search-engine summaries of pages that would not open. After the corrections above the labels are honest: 'observed' always has a run folder behind it, 'code' has been re-read in the file, 'docs' means 'Voy publishes this', and everything else is 'inferred' or 'unknown'.
